alt: Added value along the maize meal chain, per kilogram: the farm buys inputs worth US$0.12 and sells at US$0.30 (value added US$0.18); the mill buys at US$0.30 and sells at US$0.50 (US$0.20); packing and the shop buy at US$0.50 and sell at US$0.75 (US$0.25); total value added is US$0.63.
caption: Figure: each stage buys inputs and adds value; the three amounts of value added total US$0.63 a kilogram

alt: Ansoff matrix with Thandeka's four options: loyalty discount to existing shops is market penetration (lowest risk); yoghurt for the same shops is product development and milk to Gweru is market development (both medium risk); a tourist farm shop selling cheese and crafts is diversification (highest risk).
caption: Figure: Thandeka's four growth options placed on the Ansoff matrix

alt: Blake and Mouton managerial grid with concern for production across and concern for people up: Mr Banda (9,2) is close to authority-compliance, Ms Chikwanha (2,9) close to country club, Mr Dube (8,8) close to team management, and Ms Esau (1,1) is impoverished; only Mr Dube combines high concern for both.
caption: Figure: the four printing managers placed on the Blake and Mouton grid

alt: Boston matrix for Mhofu Foods: chilli sauce (relative share 1.20, growth 12%) is a star; maize meal (1.60, 2%) is a cash cow; peanut butter (0.60, 14%) is a question mark; dried fruit (0.25, 3%) is a dog. The dividing lines are relative share 1.0 and growth of 10% a year.
caption: Figure: the four Mhofu Foods products placed on the Boston matrix (bubble area is sales)

alt: Break-even chart: fixed costs are flat at US$15,000; the total cost line starts there and rises by US$1.70 a bottle; the revenue line starts at zero and rises by US$3.20 a bottle; they cross at 10,000 bottles and US$32,000. Loss to the left, profit to the right; at 12,500 bottles the margin of safety is 2,500 bottles.
caption: Figure: break-even chart for the bottle example (fixed costs US$15,000, price US$3.20, variable cost US$1.70)

alt: Monthly profit against output for three plans for Mazowe Juice: current (break-even 10,000 bottles, profit US$3,750 at 12,500), a price cut to US$2.90 (break-even 12,500, profit only US$1,800 at 14,000) and a new machine (break-even 10,000, profit US$4,500 at 12,500, but steeper losses below break-even because fixed costs are US$18,000).
caption: Figure: profit lines for the current plan, the price cut and the new machine, with expected profit marked

alt: Unit cost against capacity used for the pottery (maximum 10,000 mugs, fixed cost US$24,000, variable cost US$3): cost per mug falls from US$9.00 at 40% to US$7.00 at 60%, US$6.00 at 80% and US$5.40 at 100%; against the US$6.50 price the pottery loses money below about 6,857 mugs (69% of capacity) and profits above it.
caption: Figure: spreading fixed costs over more output lowers the cost per mug as capacity utilisation rises

alt: Closing cash balances month by month: the original forecast dips to an overdraft of US$1,250 in March and recovers to US$4,550 by June; when a major customer pays after two months the overdraft doubles to US$2,500 in March, is still US$1,450 in April, reaches nil in May and US$2,300 in June.
caption: Figure: closing cash balance in the original forecast and when one customer pays a month later

alt: Directions of communication in a hierarchy: downward arrows carry instructions, targets and feedback from the managing director through managers to staff; upward arrows carry reports, suggestions and results; a horizontal arrow links the production and sales managers at the same level, for example to agree a delivery date.
caption: Figure: downward, upward and horizontal communication in an organisation

alt: Network for Chipo's hall: A (3 days), B (4), D (6), F (5), G (4) and H (2) all have zero float and form the critical path of 24 days; C (2 days, earliest start 0, latest start 5) has 5 days of float and E (3 days, earliest start 13, latest start 15) has 2 days of float.
caption: Figure: the hall project as a network with earliest and latest times and float for each activity

alt: Two-stage decision tree for the mushroom grower: after a successful pilot (probability 0.6) rolling out has expected value US$49,500 and net US$29,500, better than staying small at US$12,000; a failed pilot (0.4) gives US$5,000; the pilot has expected value US$19,700 and net US$14,700, which beats doing nothing (US$0).
caption: Figure: the pilot-then-roll-out tree, solved from the right-hand decision first

alt: Decision tree for Tendai: build (cost US$30,000) gives US$70,000 with probability 0.6 or US$35,000 with 0.4, expected value US$56,000 and net US$26,000; upgrade (cost US$10,000) gives US$40,000 or US$22,000, expected value US$32,800 and net US$22,800; doing nothing gives US$0. Building has the highest net expected value.
caption: Figure: Tendai's decision tree with probabilities, expected values and net expected values

alt: Price rise on elastic demand: the dairy raises the price of milk from US$2.00 to US$2.20 and weekly sales fall from 5,000 to 4,000 bottles; it gains US$800 on the higher price for the 4,000 bottles still sold but loses US$2,000 on the 1,000 bottles no longer sold, so revenue falls from US$10,000 to US$8,800 (PED -2.0).
caption: Figure: revenue gained and lost when the dairy raises its price (PED of -2.0)

alt: Porter's five forces for Chipo's minibus route: rivalry is strong (many operators, the same service), new entrants are a strong threat (a second-hand vehicle is cheap), substitutes are moderate (a slower, cheaper rail service), buyers are weak individually but can switch at no cost, and suppliers are strong (few fuel suppliers), so profit in the industry is likely to be low.
caption: Figure: five forces for the Masvingo to Mutare minibus route

alt: Force field analysis for the school's phone ordering: driving forces score 4, 3 and 2 (total 9) against restraining forces of 3, 4 and 2 (total 9), so the change stalls; cutting staff fears to 1 and phone cost to 1 reduces the restraining total to 6 and the change can go ahead.
caption: Figure: force field scores before and after reducing two restraining forces

alt: Inventory control chart for Chipo's cement: stock falls 30 bags a day from the maximum of 360, reaches the re-order level of 180 on day 6 when the order is placed, and falls to the buffer of 60 bags when the delivery of 300 bags arrives after the 4-day lead time on day 10, lifting stock back to 360.
caption: Figure: the inventory control chart for cement (usage 30 a day, lead time 4 days, buffer 60, order 300)

alt: Continuum of management styles from autocratic (manager decides alone) through paternalistic (manager decides with care for staff), consultative (manager asks then decides) and participative (group decides together) to laissez-faire (employees decide for themselves): manager control falls and employee freedom rises along the line.
caption: Figure: the styles of management as a continuum from manager control to employee freedom

alt: Maslow's five levels of need (physiological, safety, social at the bottom; esteem and self-actualisation above) set beside Herzberg's factors: the lower levels resemble hygiene factors such as pay, security and relations, which prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate, while esteem and self-actualisation resemble motivators such as achievement, recognition and growth.
caption: Figure: Maslow's hierarchy compared with Herzberg's hygiene factors and motivators

alt: Matrix structure: departments (design, engineering, finance) run across the top and projects A, B and C down the side; each team member in a cell has two bosses, the department head for professional standards and pay and the project manager for the schedule, which can cause conflicting instructions.
caption: Figure: a matrix structure, where every team member sits in a department and on a project

alt: NPV of the pumping system at 10%: the inflows of US$13,500, 16,500, 18,000 and 17,000 in years 1 to 4 are worth US$12,272, 13,629, 13,518 and 11,611 in today's money (discount factors 0.909, 0.826, 0.751, 0.683); they total US$51,029.50, so after the US$46,000 outlay the NPV is plus US$5,029.50.
caption: Figure: discounting shrinks each later cash inflow; the present values total US$51,029.50 against an outlay of US$46,000

alt: Organisational chart of Nyasha's workshop: the managing director has a span of control of 3 (production, sales and finance managers); the production manager also has a span of 3 supervisors; a cutting carpenter's chain of command is carpenter (level 4), supervisor, production manager, managing director; the workers sit one level below the supervisors.
caption: Figure: the organisational chart of Nyasha's workshop, with spans of control and levels of hierarchy

alt: Cumulative cash flow for the US$72,000 poultry project: it starts at minus 72,000, is minus 51,000 after year 1, minus 24,000 after year 2, then plus 5,000 after year 3 and plus 52,000 after year 5; it crosses zero at 2.83 years, the payback period (24,000 divided by the year 3 inflow of 29,000 is 0.83).
caption: Figure: payback is the point where the cumulative cash flow reaches zero

alt: Cumulative cash flow of two US$100,000 ovens: Project A rises steadily and crosses zero after 2 years 11 months, finishing year 4 at US$36,000; Project B starts slower, crosses zero after 3 years 3 months, but its large year 4 inflow takes it higher to US$46,000, so A wins on payback and B on total return.
caption: Figure: Project A pays back sooner but Project B ends year 4 with more cash

alt: Product life cycle of the solar lamp: sales rise from 2,000 units in year 1 to a peak of 24,000 in year 5 (introduction and growth in years 1 to 4, maturity in year 5), then fall to 23,500, 19,000 and 12,000 in years 6 to 8, the decline stage; year 8 sales are half the year 5 peak.
caption: Figure: the life cycle of the Tsitsi Solar lamp, drawn from the sales table

alt: Two ways to share Masimba Brick Works' US$48,000 profit: Plan 1 pays 60% (US$28,800) in dividends, 10% (US$4,800) as a workers' bonus, 5% (US$2,400) to a community fund and keeps 25% (US$12,000); Plan 2 pays 40% (US$19,200), 25% (US$12,000), 10% (US$4,800) and keeps the same 25%, so US$9,600 moves from shareholders to workers and the community.
caption: Figure: the two plans for sharing the profit between shareholders, workers, the community and the business

alt: Profitability of two firms: Sipho's Furniture has the higher gross margin (45.0% against 25.0%) and operating margin (9.0% against 6.0%), but Rudo's Hardware has the higher return on capital employed (18.0% against 10.0%) because it earns a modest profit on a large revenue from US$400,000 of capital.
caption: Figure: the same two firms ranked differently by margins and by return on capital employed

alt: Sales forecast chart for the cold-drinks supplier: quarterly sales swing between 40 and 96 thousand bottles around a centred moving average that rises from 59.75 to 70.25 (+1.5 a quarter); extending the trend and adding the seasonal variations gives year 4 forecasts of 58.25, 80.25, 101.25 and 68.25 thousand bottles.

alt: Bar chart of the gym's expected annual revenue by segment: students US$54,000 (300 members at US$15 a month), young professionals US$144,000 (400 members at US$30) and retired people US$72,000 (300 members at US$20); young professionals give the highest revenue.
caption: Figure: expected annual revenue from each target segment (members x monthly fee x 12)

alt: The same 64 operatives organised two ways: with a span of 4 there are 4 levels (1, 4, 16 and 64 people) and 21 managers; with a span of 8 there are 3 levels (1, 8 and 64) and 9 managers, so widening the span removes a level and 12 managers.

alt: Stakeholder map for Dube Poultry's move to a river site: the bank (lender) and the council hold high power and sit in the upper half; the 40 workers have high interest but lower power; the downstream residents have strong interest but the least power until they organise. Quadrants are keep satisfied, manage closely, monitor and keep informed.
caption: Figure: where the four stakeholders sit on a power and interest map (a judgement, not a measurement)

alt: SWOT grid for Nyasha's bakery: strengths are loyal customers and a modern oven; the weakness is little cash for expansion; the opportunity is rising demand for wholesale bread from small shops; the threat is a supermarket opening nearby. The strategy matches the oven to wholesale demand and finances expansion in stages.
caption: Figure: the bakery's SWOT, with internal factors on top and external factors below

alt: Tomato market: supply S and demand D cross at US$2.00 and 300 crates; a successful advertising campaign shifts demand to D2 (200 crates more at every price), and the new equilibrium is US$2.50 and 400 crates, so price rises by US$0.50 and quantity by 100 crates.
caption: Figure: the tomato market before (E1) and after (E2) demand increases by 200 crates at every price

alt: Unit cost against output for the bottler: cost per unit falls from US$9.00 at 10,000 units to US$7.50 at 20,000 and US$6.00 at 40,000 (economies of scale), then rises to US$6.50 at 80,000 units (diseconomies of scale); the lowest cost, and best scale, is about 40,000 units.
caption: Figure: cost per unit at four outputs, showing economies then diseconomies of scale

alt: Profit bridge for Sengwa Furniture: budget profit of US$16,000 falls by US$1,500 adverse on sales revenue, US$1,500 adverse on materials and US$400 adverse on fixed overheads, and rises by US$600 favourable on labour, giving actual profit of US$13,200, US$2,800 adverse overall.
caption: Figure: from budgeted to actual profit, variance by variance (A adverse, F favourable)

alt: Flexed budget bridge: the original profit budget of US$16,000 falls US$1,200 to US$14,800 because 200 fewer desks were made; against the flexed budget, revenue is US$900 favourable, materials US$2,220 adverse, labour US$120 favourable and fixed overheads US$400 adverse, giving actual profit of US$13,200, so the true profit variance is US$1,600 adverse and materials are the real problem.
caption: Figure: separating the volume effect (US$1,200) from the cost and price variances once the budget is flexed

alt: Nyasha's bakery: current assets of US$16,000 (inventory 8,400, receivables 6,100, cash 1,500) less current liabilities of US$9,200 (payables 5,200, overdraft 3,000, tax 1,000) leave working capital of US$6,800, but only US$1,500 of the assets is cash while US$3,000 is an overdraft repayable on demand.
caption: Figure: working capital is current assets less current liabilities, but most of the assets are not cash
